doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: The repertory orchestra with Dick Hyman
summary: He plays in a jazz repertory group, performing Blanton and Alpert pieces.

blocks.x: Yeah. It’s an interesting little thing. We have a repertory orchestra. There’s another jazz society in the Fort Lauderdale area called the Gold Coast Jazz Society that used to be booked by a very capable woman named Lee Amley who has since passed away. And their board is a board. They can’t seem to decide what their actual thrust is, whether it’s music or — well I haven’t been that — I used to advise them on some things, but I’ve been too busy on this other one now. Anyway we’re doing a concert over there with Dick and there’s a guitar player down in south Florida by the name of Simon Saults who organized a — it’s either a seven or eight piece group depending on whether we have a baritone sax or not, to do repertory material, jazz repertory, all the old Louis Armstrong things. When Dick is the pianist — we started out as a local group sponsored by the Gold Coast Jazz Society, so we had the unwieldy name of the Gold Coast Jazz Society Repertory Ensemble Orchestra, or something like that. Anyway I call it the Rep Work — a repertory orchestra. We do old stuff, historical jazz, and I’ll play “Jack the Bear” the first bass solo from Jimmy Blanton with Duke, and I do a piece called “Trigger Fantasy” with them which was written by Trigger Alpert — he lives in Punta Gorda Florida now I think — sorry, Trigger, if that’s not right — a piece that Dick arranged in the sixties for a Riverside record session under Trigger’s name. There’s a whole funny story that goes — a string of coincidences kind of story that goes with that but it’s too long for here. But I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -22-

do that with him and they do a trumpet feature that Chris LaBarbara, a very excellent trumpet player over there, he’s like Mister Repertory, he can imitate anybody. I mean he can do Harry James, he can do Louis, and he can do Roy Eldridge very well, and you name it. And it’s an interesting thing. So then we add Dick in there, Dick comes out and does all his little stride things, the Jelly Rollisms, and I mean Dick is the living embodiment of the Encyclopedia of Jazz at his fingertips. I mean there is nobody that has more of that kind of knowledge than Dick Hyman, and can also play it. So that’s always a lot of fun.
